newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Inflation, retail sales data.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Inflation, retail sales data.

text.p: After weathering Friday's payrolls storm, the U.S. credit market can now turn its attention to next week's August retail sales and inflation reports.

Producer and consumer price reports, due at 0830 EDT/1330 GMT on Thursday and Friday, respectively, are expected to be market friendly, although economists said the overall inflation picture remains a concern in light of the August employment data.
Mounting signs of wage pressures may force the Fed's hand come September 24, but August wholesale and consumer prices should remain under control.

"The bottom line is that even though the August inflation numbers next week should look fairly subdued, I would be worried longer term if I were the Fed," said Mike Penzer, senior economist at Bank of America.

"In the coming months higher oil prices will push inflation a little higher, but longer term, with rapid job growth and a falling unemployment rate, wages accelerate and with a lag the CPI should as well," he added.
Economists surveyed by Reuters are calling for 0.1 percent gains in overall and core producer prices for August, and 0.2 percent gains in overall and core consumer prices.

Retail sales, due Friday at 0830 EDT/1330 GMT, are expected to get an ample boost from strong August auto sales, and therefore could generate more price action than the inflation numbers, economists said.

"Clearly in the last couple of days, in view of the strength we got in auto sales, people have revised up their numbers," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.
"We expect a rise of 1.0 percent with the bulk of the strength concentrated in autos."
Consensus forecasts have retail sales rising 0.7 percent in August.

The Federal Reserve's beige book, a survey of economic activity in each of the Fed's regions, should also generate some interest, when it is released at 1200 EDT/1600 GMT on Wednesday, economists said.
The issue of wage pressures has been prominently featured in recent Fed beige books and is likely to garner added attention in the upcoming report.

"I think it will show more of the same -- which is some pressure on wages, the economy moving ahead and not showing a lot of signs of slowing down," said Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney Inc.

Next week, Held said, the market could reassess its reaction to the past week's data regardless of how the numbers play out. He said Friday's gains were largely a relief trade, and did not reflect the fundamentals.
"The fact of the matter is the economy is still growing at a reasonable clip and at a clip that's too fast to alleviate wage pressures," Held said.
He expects the federal funds rate to rise to 5.75 percent from its current 5.25 percent by the end of the year.

The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond was up 15/32 at 95-16/32 to yield 7.11 percent in late Friday trading. The federal funds rate is expected to open at 5-1/4 percent on Monday, in line with the Fed's target for the rate.
